summary: This work co-designs ultra-high-rate quantum low-density parity-check codes with reconfigurable neutral-atom hardware, achieving encoding rates exceeding $1/2$ at block lengths $\sim 1000$ qubits by constraining affine permutation matrices to commute with reference maps whose orbits decompose into simple atom rearrangements. Circuit-level simulations at $p = 0.1\%$ yield per-logical-per-round error rates of $1.3_{-0.9}^{+3.0} \times 10^{-13}$ for the $[[2304,1156,\leq 14]]$ code and $2.9_{-1.5}^{+3.1} \times 10^{-11}$ for the $[[1152,580,\leq 12]]$ code using a hierarchical decoder combining belief propagation with integer-programming fallback.
motivation: Quantum error correction requires reducing qubit overhead; quantum LDPC codes promise high rates exceeding $1/10$, but prior constructions achieved only $\sim 1/10$ at practical block lengths, and it was unclear whether Kasai's recent ultra-high-rate affine-permutation construction (rate $\sim 1/2$, distance $>30$ at $n \sim 9000$) could yield competitive performance on near-term platforms with realistic hardware constraints.
method: Starting from Kasai's block-circulant CSS construction over affine permutations $x \mapsto ax + b \pmod{P}$, we identify codes where all transition permutations commute with a reference APM, decomposing into orbit-wise cyclic shifts plus small inter-orbit permutations compilable into $2$–$3$ crossed-AOD moves rather than $O(\log P)$ moves. Finite-size search enforces girth $\geq 6$, structured transitions, and verified distance bounds, yielding instances with rates $\approx 0.50$ at $n \in \{1152, 2304, 4608\}$.
result: The $[[2304,1156,\leq 14]]$ code achieves logical error rate $1.3_{-0.9}^{+3.0} \times 10^{-13}$ per logical qubit per round at circuit-level noise $p = 0.1\%$ with 392 million shots (1 error observed), approaching the teraquop regime; codes lie near the Pareto frontier predicted by heuristic finite-blocklength estimates, with syndrome extraction completing in $\sim 8$–$10$ ms using realistic atom transport.
